notes.detailedSummary: Fixes proper primary reference data, defines bounded inputs in the actual decreasing completion, admits zero and mixed-zero inputs belonging to that class, and excludes all bottom/unbounded inputs. Uses only the supplied independent cone/comparison, compact topology, density, and full descent. Dimension zero is empty and curves have zero potential entries.
notes.text:
# n1. Domain, reference data, and the retained grant

This manuscript is a partial result for P12.4, not a solution claim. The only supplied result used is qualified G331, including its entire source, mandatory annotation, source ledger, and exact scope. ROOT338 is an unreviewed approach, not a premise. No envelope, intersection, product, energy, locality, or arbitrary-model cofinality theorem is imported from G331.

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be excellent, reduced, local, and of positive dimension $n$. Put $X_{\mathfrak a}=\{v:v(\mathfrak a)=1\}$ for a fixed proper $\mathfrak m$-primary ideal $\mathfrak a$. A point is a centred real semivaluation on $R$ with $0<v(\mathfrak m)<\infty$; its prime support may be nonminimal. Every such support is retained, including supports on the conductor quotient. Ideal values mean minima on a finite generating set. In particular primary ideal values are finite, positive, continuous, and bounded on $X_{\mathfrak a}$. Units have value zero. G331 gives the compact Hausdorff boundary and the exact primary change $T(v)=v/v(\mathfrak b)$.

The geometric core was defined before ideal closure: actual negative effective finite REAL Cartier presentations on actual primary blowups, with nonnegative degree on every contracted proper integral curve. G331 proves that its uniform closure $C=C_{\rm geom}$ equals the uniform closure of finite nonnegative real combinations of $-v(I)$, where $I$ is primary or the unit ideal. Its completion $D=D_{\rm geom}$ consists of infima of ACTUAL nonempty decreasing $C$-nets, with the identically $-\infty$ function allowed. We use only this completion, not closure under arbitrary infima, increasing limits, or flattened nested nets.

The product-input domain in this manuscript is
$$D^{\rm bd}_{\mathfrak a}=\{u\in D:-M\le u\le0\text{ for some finite }M\}.$$
This includes every bounded real, discontinuous completed input, zero, and permitted mixed-zero branch patterns. It excludes every input having a $-\infty$ value, including bottom. Every continuous input in $C$ is bounded. Existence of a bounded decreasing representation needs no truncation: if $g_\alpha\downarrow u$ and $u\ge-M$, then $g_\alpha\ge u\ge-M$ and $g_\alpha\le0$.

Use $p=n-1$ potential entries; a test supplies the nth intersection entry. For non-equidimensional $R$, all algebraic moments below use the degree-$n$ part of the primary length polynomial. Lower-dimensional components remain in the boundary and domain, but contribute zero in this chosen convention. A separate lower-dimensional product would have a different arity; none is silently added. In dimension one there are zero potentials and a reference measure, constructed geometrically in n5. For dimension zero the reduced local ring is a field, the centred boundary is empty, and the measure is the unique zero measure; there is no negative-arity assertion.

G331 also supplies two specific functional facts used below. Rational profiles $-v(I)/k$ with $k\in\mathbb N_{>0}$ (unit allowed) are uniformly dense in $C$. The rational difference span of ideal gauges is a lattice, contains rational constants since $v(\mathfrak a)=1$, and is uniformly dense in $C(X_{\mathfrak a},\mathbb R)$. To recall the mechanism, a common denominator turns any span element into $(v(J)-v(K))/k$, and
$$\min(v(I)-v(J),v(K)-v(H))=v(IH+KJ)-v(JH).$$
The bounded truncations $v((f)+\mathfrak a^N)=\min(v(f),N)$ separate all semivaluations, including infinite coordinates. Uniform closure of this rational lattice is a real vector lattice; the compact lattice approximation argument yields all real continuous tests. This is density on the entire compact boundary, not a finite grid.

For a finite normalization $R\hookrightarrow S$, G331 retains the disjoint local normal centres above $\mathfrak m$ and their FULL restriction fibres. At finite conductor value the fibre is a singleton. At infinite conductor value the identification is exactly equality on the conductor quotient. Continuous and completed geometric functions descend precisely when constant on these whole fibres. We do not select one lift or discard an infinity stratum. Normalization in n4 is applied only to actual pullbacks of downstairs functions.

For nonreduced germs the present data are those of the reduction and the reduced gauge. No nilpotent generic length is reconstructed; n6 proves an explicit obstruction to doing so from these data alone. P12.5 energy and general finite-map geometric operators in P12.6 are outside the results here.

The paper and local notes give mathematical draft arguments; hashing, compilation, and finite diagnostics are separate evidence. The entire G331 source/annotation/ledger are retained under inputs/mathematical. Rerun data retention: `python audit_inputs.py`. New source applications are recorded in source-application-ledger.md.

notes.summary: Proves the all-support primary mixed-multiplicity kernel and positivity at arbitrary field/characteristic; no geometric intersection or locality conclusion.
notes.detailedSummary: Proves symmetry, product/power linearity, single-slot inclusion monotonicity via simultaneous superficial choices, integral-closure invariance via a finite graded algebra/ray-polynomial argument, and full-boundary valuative well-definedness. Exact current Swanson--Huneke immediate units and finite residue-field transfer are qualified. Unit slots have zero moments, lower-dimensional components contribute zero by convention.
notes.text:
# n2. An unconditional primary mixed-multiplicity kernel

Use the domain and full-boundary conventions of n1. This note proves the algebraic kernel needed for moment measures, with arbitrary characteristic, residue field, non-Cohen--Macaulay rings, and non-equidimensional reduced components allowed. It proves no geometric Monge--Ampere operator.

Here are the precise published applications. In the CURRENT July 2024 author version of Swanson--Huneke, Theorem 17.4.2 says that for a Noetherian local ring, finite module $M$, and primary ideals $I_1,\ldots,I_s$, the function $\ell_R(M/I_1^{t_1}\cdots I_s^{t_s}M)$ is a rational polynomial of total degree $\dim M$ for all sufficiently large independent integer $t_i$. Definition 17.4.3 takes its degree-$\dim R$ coefficients, using factorial denominators, as mixed multiplicities; they are zero if $\dim M<\dim R$. These statements and their full immediate proof were read. We use this degree convention even when components have different dimensions.

The complete 17.2.2 proof gives a nonempty Zariski open set of choices for a superficial element in $I_1/\mathfrak m I_1$, with finitely many prescribed primes avoidable when $I_1$ is not contained in them. Complete 17.2.4 and 17.4.6 show that a superficial element $x\in I_1$ avoiding the minimal primes reduces a mixed multiplicity having at least one $I_1$ entry to the corresponding mixed multiplicity over $R/xR$ with that entry removed, when $\dim R>1$. No regular sequence or Cohen--Macaulay hypothesis is required. The finite annihilator correction in dimension one is part of the source, but we do not need that formula to compare the last ideal.

Finite residue fields cause no restriction. Pass to $R(Z)=R[Z]_{\mathfrak m R[Z]}$ solely for these algebraic proofs. Lemma 8.4.2 gives faithful flatness, equal dimension, preservation of primary ideals and lengths. Explicitly, a composition series of any finite-length $R$-module tensors to a series with factors $\kappa(\mathfrak m)(Z)$, so its length is unchanged. Thus every multigraded length polynomial and its coefficients are unchanged. No identification of boundaries across this transcendental extension is used.

Write $e_R(I_1,\ldots,I_n)$ for the coefficient with one entry of each ideal. Product and power linearity follow directly from the polynomial: replace the variables for $I$ and $J$ by the same variable to represent $(IJ)^t$. The coefficient with exponent one in that variable and one in the other $n-1$ variables receives exactly the terms with exponent one in $I$ or in $J$. Hence
$$e_R(IJ,I_2,\ldots,I_n)=e_R(I,I_2,\ldots,I_n)+e_R(J,I_2,\ldots,I_n),$$
and $e_R(I^r,I_2,\ldots,I_n)=r e_R(I,I_2,\ldots,I_n)$. Relabelling gives symmetry. If an ideal is the unit ideal, its length polynomial is independent of that variable, so the corresponding mixed multiplicity is zero. This convention is compatible with the identities.

We give the single-slot inclusion proof, rather than trying to compare individual coefficients of unequal multivariate polynomials. Suppose $J\subset K$ are primary and the other $n-1$ ideals are fixed. Over an infinite residue field, choose in the second slot an element superficial for BOTH tuples $(I_2,I_3,\ldots,I_n,J)$ and $(I_2,I_3,\ldots,I_n,K)$, and avoiding all minimal primes. The two allowed sets are nonempty opens in the same finite-dimensional vector space $I_2/\mathfrak m I_2$, obtained by removing finitely many proper subspaces in the 17.2.2 proof. Their intersection still has a rational point over an infinite field. The avoidance conditions can be included in that finite union. Each quotient has dimension one less: avoiding the minimal primes gives the upper bound, and lifting a system of parameters from the quotient and using the height theorem gives the lower bound. The quotient images of $J,K$ remain primary and included. Apply 17.4.6 to both tuples. Repeat in the remaining fixed slots, choosing simultaneous superficial elements afresh in each quotient. In dimension one, $J^N\subset K^N$ gives
$$\ell(R/J^N)\ge\ell(R/K^N),\qquad e(J)\ge e(K)$$
by dividing by $N$ and using the one-variable Hilbert--Samuel polynomial. Thus, in every dimension,
$$J\subset K\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e_R(J,I_2,\ldots,I_n)\ge e_R(K,I_2,\ldots,I_n).$$
The same reduction to a one-dimensional primary multiplicity proves positivity for primary slots. The positivity of the last one-variable leading coefficient is Theorem 11.1.3 and Definition 11.1.5, whose immediate proof/context were read. Unit slots give zero. These arguments also work for the nonreduced quotients created by superficial elements.

Integral-closure invariance has a separate proof. If $K\subset\overline J$, put $L=J+K$. Each degree-one generator $xt$ of $R[Lt]$ is integral over $R[Jt]$ by its homogeneous ideal-integrality equation. Thus $R[Lt]$ is a finite graded $R[Jt]$-module. A finite homogeneous generating list, with degrees at most $h$, gives $L^{t+h}\subset J^t$ for all $t\ge1$: its degree $t+h$ coefficients lie in $J^{t+h-d}\subset J^t$. Also $J^t\subset L^t$. After multiplying by any fixed products $A=I_2^{t_2}\cdots I_s^{t_s}$, this gives
$$\ell(R/L^tA)\le\ell(R/J^tA)\le\ell(R/L^{t+h}A).$$
On every ray of positive integral exponents, divide by the common large parameter to the power $n$. The two outside polynomials have the same degree-$n$ homogeneous part; the fixed shift $h$ contributes only smaller degrees. Thus the degree-$n$ parts for $J$ and $L$ agree on every positive rational ray and therefore as polynomials. All mixed coefficients agree. If $J,K$ have equal integral closure, apply this twice to $J+K$. This proves invariance without transferring coefficient inequalities from a length inequality. The finite graded argument is proved here and does not require finite normalization of a Rees algebra.

Finally, the order used in these moments is the order of functions on ALL $X_{\mathfrak a}$. For primary or unit $J,K$,
$$v(K)\ge v(J)\text{ on }X_{\mathfrak a}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K\subset\overline J.$$
For proper primary $J$, apply the complete Swanson--Huneke 6.8.4 centred rank-one DVR criterion to each domain $R/P$ for $P\in\operatorname{Min}R$. Each quotient has positive dimension: in a positive-dimensional reduced local ring the maximal ideal cannot be minimal. Normalize these DVRs by the nonzero primary image of $\mathfrak a$; they are actual points of $X_{\mathfrak a}$ with support $P$. Then 6.8.3 (or 1.1.5 componentwise integral dependence) assembles the conclusion. Conversely a monic ideal-integrality equation and the unique-smallest-term argument in the quotient by any semivaluation support give the inequality at that support; primary values are finite. For $J=R$ the conclusion is automatic. For $K=R$ and proper $J$ the inequality is impossible on the nonempty section. These cover unit cases. Nonminimal supports are not removed merely because the criterion can be tested on a subset.

For rational profiles $u_i=-v(I_i)/k_i$ and a primary ideal test $v(J)$, define
$$B_{\boldsymbol u}(v(J))=\frac{e_R(I_1,\ldots,I_p,J)}{k_1\cdots k_p}.$$
For $p=0$ this means $e_R(J)$. A zero input may be represented by the unit ideal and gives zero if $p\ge1$. Equal rational profiles have, after integer powers, equal primary ideal values, hence equal integral closures; invariance and power linearity make the definition independent of presentation. Any rational linear relation among ideal tests becomes $v(A)=v(B)$ after synchronizing denominators and multiplying ideals, so the same argument makes the test functional well-defined. If a rational test function $v(A)-v(B)$ is nonnegative, the criterion gives $A\subset\overline B$. Since $A+B$ has the same integral closure as $B$, inclusion monotonicity and invariance give $e(\boldsymbol I,A)\ge e(\boldsymbol I,B)$. Thus the functional is positive on the whole rational test lattice.

Input order also follows: $u\le w$ implies the moments for $u$ are at least those for $w$ in that slot. For $u=-v(I)/k,w=-v(J)/l$, use $I^l\subset\overline{J^k}$ and divide by $kl$. All slots are symmetric and additive on addition of negative rational profiles. These are the algebraic kernel and order laws, not Cartier intersection comparison or locality.

Source bodies/hashes/URLs and the exact units used are retained in inputs/primary, reports/input-hashes.json, and source-application-ledger.md. Rerun: `python audit_inputs.py`; `python build_delivery.py`. No program establishes these universal proofs.

notes.summary: Constructs positive bounded moment measures for real C and actual bounded D inputs, with representation independence and weak descending-net continuity; these are not yet actual geometric products.
notes.detailedSummary: Gives mass and negative-shift error bounds, extends rational moments to real continuous tuples and then every bounded actual decreasing-net completion tuple, without increasing closure or flattening. Proves additivity, order on ideal moments, majorant supremum formula, and weak descending-net convergence for a common bounded net with a specified limit in D. Does not prove measure-order monotonicity, total variation convergence, independent Cartier comparison, or locality.
notes.text:
# n3. Bounded real and actual decreasing-net moment measures

Use n1 and the proved algebraic kernel n2. This note constructs finite positive Radon MOMENT measures $\nu_{\mathfrak a}(u_1,\ldots,u_p)$ on the entire boundary for every tuple in $(D^{\rm bd}_{\mathfrak a})^p$. The name deliberately does not assert the geometric intersection/locality properties still missing in n7. The proof covers arbitrary real continuous and bounded completed functions, not just rational profiles.

For a rational tuple from n2 its positive functional on the rational test lattice has mass
$$B_{\boldsymbol u}(1)=B_{\boldsymbol u}(v(\mathfrak a))=\frac{e_R(I_1,\ldots,I_p,\mathfrak a)}{\prod k_i}.$$
If $q>\|f\|_\infty$ is rational, $q\pm f$ are nonnegative lattice tests. Positivity gives $|B(f)|\le qB(1)$, hence $|B(f)|\le\|f\|_\infty B(1)$. Uniform density from n1 extends this rational functional uniquely to a bounded real-linear functional on all real continuous functions: real linearity follows by rational approximation of scalars and norm continuity. Positivity persists by approximating a nonnegative continuous function and adding a vanishing positive rational constant to the approximation. The compact-Hausdorff Riesz correspondence identifies it with a finite positive regular Borel (Radon) measure. Equivalently, in the convention explicitly used in BFJ Section 4.2, a Radon measure is its positive continuous test functional. The Riesz correspondence is ordinary functional background at exactly compact Hausdorff hypotheses, not an extra geometric positivity theorem.

There is a uniform bound on gauge moments. If $-M\le u_i\le0$ for every rational entry, order comparison with the constant $-M$ (first take rational constants just above $M$) gives
$$0\le B_{\boldsymbol u}(v(J))\le M^p e_R(\mathfrak a^{[p]},J),\qquad \nu_{\mathfrak a}(\boldsymbol u)(X_{\mathfrak a})\le M^p e_R(\mathfrak a).$$
Here brackets mean repeated ENTRIES, not ideal exponentiation; $e_R(\mathfrak a)=e_R(\mathfrak a^{[n]})$. For $p=0$ the factor is one. No order of measures, as opposed to order on ideal-gauge moments, is asserted.

The decisive error estimate uses legitimate negative constants in $C$. For rational tuples $\boldsymbol u,\boldsymbol w$ in $[-M,0]$ with coordinatewise sup-norm difference at most $\varepsilon$, use $u_i-\varepsilon\le w_i$ and the reverse inequalities, with a rational slightly larger error if necessary. Expanding the additive kernel after adding $-\varepsilon=-\varepsilon v(\mathfrak a)$ in each slot gives
$$\left|B_{\boldsymbol u}(v(J))-B_{\boldsymbol w}(v(J))\right|\le [(M+\varepsilon)^p-M^p]e_R(\mathfrak a^{[p]},J).\tag{1}$$
Indeed each nonempty subset of shifted slots contributes a nonnegative term bounded by $\varepsilon^{|S|}M^{p-|S|}e_R(\mathfrak a^{[p]},J)$; summing them is the binomial expression. For $p=0$ the expression is zero.

Now take arbitrary REAL $C$ inputs and approximate each uniformly by rational profiles using n1. The approximants may lie in $[-M-1,0]$, which supplies a common bound. Estimate (1) makes every ideal-test moment Cauchy and independent of approximation. Every rational lattice test is a difference of such gauges, so its functional values converge. Positivity and the mass bound pass to the limit, hence give a measure by the preceding extension argument. Finite uniform density then proves weak convergence on every continuous test. The same estimate with arbitrarily slightly larger bounds/errors passes to the real $C$ inputs. Symmetry, nonnegative real homogeneity, additivity within the negative cone, and order on ideal-gauge moments pass to the limit. For additivity use rational approximations of each summand and their sum, and for real homogeneity approximate the scalar rationally. These are properties of the proved moment functional; the proof does not cite BFJ 4.4 outside its smooth range.

For each $u_i\in D^{\rm bd}_{\mathfrak a}$ choose an ACTUAL decreasing $C$-net $g_{i,\alpha_i}\downarrow u_i$. By n1 all its terms have the bound $[-M,0]$ if the tuple has that bound. The finite Cartesian product of the directed index sets represents the mixed tuple. For every ideal test $v(J)$, its moments increase under refinement and stay bounded by the preceding estimate. Define $B_{\boldsymbol u}(v(J))$ as their finite supremum. This is an increasing limit of bounded SCALARS, not an increasing limit in the function class. Values for difference tests converge by subtraction. Positive test functionals and their common mass bound pass to the limit on the rational lattice and extend to a finite positive measure as before.

We prove representation independence without a flattening assumption. Let $g_{i,\alpha_i}$ and $f_{i,\beta_i}$ represent the same bounded tuple. Fix a tuple of indices $\boldsymbol\beta$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Since $u_i\le f_{i,\beta_i}$, the directed open sets
$$\{g_{i,\alpha_i}<f_{i,\beta_i}+\varepsilon\}$$
cover the compact space. A finite subcover and directedness select one $\alpha_i$ for which the inequality holds everywhere. Do this for each of the finitely many slots. Then $g_{i,\alpha_i}-\varepsilon\le f_{i,\beta_i}$. Moment order and the real $C$ negative-shift expansion give
$$B_{\boldsymbol f_{\beta}}(v(J))\le B_{\boldsymbol g_{\alpha}-\varepsilon}(v(J))\le \sup_{\boldsymbol\alpha}B_{\boldsymbol g_{\alpha}}(v(J))+[(M+\varepsilon)^p-M^p]e_R(\mathfrak a^{[p]},J).$$
Take the supremum over $\boldsymbol\beta$, send $\varepsilon$ to zero, and reverse the roles. Equality of every gauge moment, density, and the mass bound give equality of the measures. The same argument, now with limit tuples satisfying $u_i\le w_i$ and fixed continuous terms majorizing $w_i$, proves order on ideal-gauge moments throughout the bounded $D$ domain.

Addition of two actual decreasing $C$-nets, indexed by their finite product, gives an actual decreasing $C$-net to their sum. Thus the sum belongs to $D$ by its definition, with a finite bound. Taking scalar moment limits in the $C$ additivity identity proves additivity on bounded $D$ entries. Scaling is handled the same way; scalar zero produces zero. Symmetry is immediate. In particular the negative-constant shift expansion and (1) are now valid on bounded $D$ inputs. No closure under arbitrary $D$ infima or arbitrary nested-net flattening was invoked.

The useful exact formula, for every ideal $J$, is
$$B_{\boldsymbol u}(v(J))=\sup\{B_{\boldsymbol g}(v(J)):g_i\in C,\ g_i\ge u_i\text{ for all }i\}.\tag{2}$$
Every such $g_i$ lies in the common bound $[-M,0]$. The order just proved gives the upper bound; the terms of any representing nets give the reverse bound. This is a formula for scalar moments, not a new definition of $D$ by all majorants.

Here is the precise descending-net theorem. Let $\lambda$ range over one directed set, let $u_{i,\lambda}\in D^{\rm bd}_{\mathfrak a}$ decrease pointwise to a SPECIFIED $u_i\in D^{\rm bd}_{\mathfrak a}$, and suppose all entries and limits have a common finite bound $[-M,0]$. Then
$$\nu_{\mathfrak a}(u_{1,\lambda},\ldots,u_{p,\lambda})\ \longrightarrow\ \nu_{\mathfrak a}(u_1,\ldots,u_p)$$
weakly, for the net. The membership of the limit is an actual hypothesis; no new infimum closure is being claimed. To prove it, order gives a bound above by the target gauge moment. Fix a continuous majorant tuple $g_i\ge u_i$. Every $D$ function is upper semicontinuous, so $\{u_{i,\lambda}<g_i+\varepsilon\}$ is open. The decreasing net gives a directed cover; compactness selects one common $\lambda$ for all slots with $u_{i,\lambda}-\varepsilon\le g_i$. Thus
$$B_{\boldsymbol u_\lambda}(v(J))\ge B_{\boldsymbol g}(v(J))-[(M+\varepsilon)^p-M^p]e_R(\mathfrak a^{[p]},J).$$
First send $\varepsilon$ to zero, then take the supremum in (2). The gauge moments converge to the target moments. They determine convergence for the rational difference lattice; density and the uniform mass bound extend it to every continuous test. This proves the actual weak descending-net theorem for this moment construction. It is not convergence in total variation, and it is not locality.

All-zero inputs yield zero for $p\ge1$, and any single globally zero entry annihilates the mixed measure. For mixed-zero patterns on normalization branches, the whole tuple is still in the stated domain if it belongs to G331's class; this construction makes no strict-negativity exclusion. It is not extended here to unbounded or bottom inputs.

Artifacts: n3.md, argument.md, P12.4-paper.tex, and native-notes.json. Rerun: `python build_delivery.py`. The conclusion is a unique bounded moment extension with the displayed laws. Independent Cartier comparison and actual open-set locality remain separate obligations.

notes.summary: Exact one-factor primary-gauge change and residue-degree normalization for moment measures; full bounded BFJ comparison only in its published smooth characteristic-zero closed-germ range.
notes.detailedSummary: Proves nu_b=T_*[v_a(b) nu_a], coefficient-wise normalization over actual top-dimensional normal centres with residue-degree weights and no vertical generic degree, and equality with the published BFJ operator on all bounded inputs/all semivaluations at smooth affine closed germs over algebraically closed characteristic-zero fields. Neither singular Cartier comparison nor locality is imported from BFJ Section 4.
notes.text:
# n4. Exact gauge, normalization, and published smooth comparison for moments

Use G331 and n1--n3. This note concerns the moment measures proved there. The rules are genuine identities for those measures, but do not fill the missing singular Cartier comparison or locality theorem.

For two proper PRIMARY gauges $\mathfrak a,\mathfrak b$, let $d(v)=v(\mathfrak b)$ on $X_{\mathfrak a}$ and $T(v)=v/d(v)$. The function $d$ is continuous and bounded above and away from zero. For each degree-one homogeneous input set $u_{i,\mathfrak b}(T(v))=u_{i,\mathfrak a}(v)/d(v)$. G331 proves that this transports both $C$ and actual $D$ representations. Bounds remain finite, and uniform convergence transports because $1/d$ is bounded. Then the EXACT measure change for the moment construction is
$$\nu_{\mathfrak b}(\boldsymbol u_{\mathfrak b})=T_*\big[d\,\nu_{\mathfrak a}(\boldsymbol u_{\mathfrak a})\big].\tag{3}$$
For a rational ideal tuple and a gauge test $v_{\mathfrak b}(J)$, the right side pairs to
$$\int d(v)\frac{v(J)}{d(v)}\,d\nu_{\mathfrak a}=\frac{e_R(I_1,\ldots,I_p,J)}{\prod k_i},$$
which is the left moment. Density of the test lattice gives equality of measures. Uniform and actual descending continuity from n3 then prove (3) for all bounded inputs in $D$. Multiplication of tests by the fixed continuous bounded $d$ commutes with those weak limits. This is one factor of $d$, not $d^n$ or $d^{-(n-1)}$. For $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak a^r$, the same ray has $d=r$, the potentials on its new section divide by $r$, and the transported measure multiplies by $r$. The cocycle follows by substitution. There is no nonprimary denominator anywhere.

Let $S$ be the finite normalization of reduced excellent $R$, and let $q$ run over all its local normal centres above $\mathfrak m$. Put $S_q$ for the corresponding normal local domain, $f_q=[\kappa(q):\kappa(\mathfrak m)]$, and $\rho_q:X_{\mathfrak a S_q}\to X_{\mathfrak a}$ for restriction. Use only centres with $\dim S_q=n$ in the degree-$n$ formula:
$$\nu_{\mathfrak a,R}(\boldsymbol u)=\sum_{q:\dim S_q=n} f_q\,\rho_{q,*}\nu_{\mathfrak a S_q,S_q}(\rho_q^*\boldsymbol u).\tag{4}$$
All other centres and all semivaluation supports are retained; a centre of smaller dimension has zero top-degree contribution in this convention, rather than a fictitious degree assigned to it.

Here is the algebraic proof. Complete Swanson--Huneke 17.4.4 gives additivity of mixed multiplicity on exact sequences of finite modules, and complete 17.4.8 gives the sum over maximal-dimensional minimal primes with coefficient $\ell(M_P)$. Applied to $M=R,S$, the coefficients at every minimal $P$ of $R$ are both one: a reduced ring localized at a minimal prime is its component field, and normalization is generically the same product of fields. Hence $e_R(\boldsymbol I;R)=e_R(\boldsymbol I;S)$. Alternatively $S/R$ is annihilated by a regular conductor element and has dimension less than $n$, so additivity gives the same identity. For each product $A=I_1^{t_1}\cdots I_s^{t_s}$, the finite Artinian quotient $S/AS$ splits into its local factors. A finite-length $S_q$ composition series has $R$-length $f_q$ per factor, so
$$\ell_R(S/AS)=\sum_q f_q\ell_{S_q}(S_q/AS_q).$$
Compare degree-$n$ homogeneous coefficients using 17.4.2. Terms with $\dim S_q<n$ are zero; this gives
$$e_R(I_1,\ldots,I_n)=\sum_{q:\dim S_q=n} f_q e_{S_q}(I_1S_q,\ldots,I_nS_q).$$
Formula (4) follows on rational tuples from the gauge moments and test density, and on $C$ and bounded $D$ tuples by the proved continuities. Pullback of each chosen decreasing representation is an actual bounded decreasing representation on each centre, by G331. There are finitely many centres, so summation commutes with the limits.

This proof checks actual residue degrees, including inseparable ones. It uses generic identity of normalization on reduced component fields, not an invented vertical degree and not a general finite-map trace theorem. On the conductor-infinite stratum every normalization point is still present. Formula (4) pushes all of them down, adding any masses whose fibres are identified. The downstairs inputs restrict with identical values on the entire fibre, by their actual pullback, and the formula is unaffected by descriptions of that fibre. No assertion of automatic descent of arbitrary upstairs operator data is made. General finite maps/P12.6 remain separate.

At the EXACT published BFJ range there is an additional comparison. Let the germ be at a smooth CLOSED point of a smooth affine variety over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, of dimension $n\ge2$, with $\mathfrak a=\mathfrak m$. G331 identifies $C,D$ with the full BFJ classes on all semivaluations, with bottom adjoined; our bounded domain excludes bottom. BFJ's setting was read at its actual hypotheses. Its complete Section 4 was read, including proofs of 4.1--4.9. It defines the independent Cartier intersection, gives
$$-\langle Z(I_1),\ldots,Z(I_n)\rangle=e_R(I_1,\ldots,I_n),$$
and in Proposition 4.6 characterizes its mixed measure by pairing psh test functions with that intersection. Proposition 4.4 proves symmetry, additivity, order, and continuity of nef intersections; its proof and Remark 4.5 explicitly use smooth multiplier approximation for additivity. Proposition 4.7 gives the ideal moments, 4.8 decreasing-sequence weak continuity, and 4.9 the model-atom formula. These are NOT applied at a singular/positive-characteristic germ.

The polynomial mixed multiplicity in n2 agrees here with BFJ's generic-length convention: choose a superficial parameter sequence in the given ideals, as in complete SH 17.4.7. The local ring is regular, hence Cohen--Macaulay, so the successive parameter elements are nonzerodivisors. Repeated SH 17.4.6 reduces to its dimension-one formula, whose annihilator term is zero. The coefficient is therefore the length of the generic parameter quotient, exactly the convention in BFJ (4.3). This equality of conventions is used only in this regular range.

On rational ideal tuples, BFJ 4.7 consequently gives exactly n2's gauge moments, so test density identifies its measure with $\nu_{\mathfrak m}$. For $C$ tuples use uniform rational approximation. The order of BFJ intersections and their additivity give the same negative-shift estimate (1), hence uniform weak convergence, and equality follows. Finally let $g_{i,\alpha_i}\downarrow u_i$ be any actual bounded decreasing $C$ representations of bounded BFJ inputs. Their associated Weil coefficients decrease to those of $u_i$ at every divisorial valuation. Proposition 4.4's continuity along decreasing families applies to this finite product net, with the fixed Cartier test $Z(J)$. Its proof gives families, not just sequences: the intersection is upper semicontinuous in the coefficient topology and monotone, and a coordinatewise decreasing net converges in that topology. Thus the gauge moments converge to those of the BFJ measure. N3 and density identify $\nu$ with BFJ on EVERY bounded completed input and ALL semivaluations. For another primary gauge, equation (3) transports this comparison; it does not attribute an unstated arbitrary-gauge theorem to BFJ.

BFJ's exact smooth intersection comparison is inherited in this range because the moment measure was identified with its published operator. Its Section 4 contains no general open-set locality statement used here. We make no new claim that this argument proves locality, even at this published range. Curve/DVR and empty dimension-zero conventions are n5/n1.

notes.text:
# n5. Actual geometric curve reference measure and dimension-zero convention

Use qualified G331 and n1--n4. Here there IS an actual independent Cartier intersection comparison and locality theorem, in the exact range of every excellent reduced local CURVE, with arbitrary characteristic and residue field. Arity is zero, so this is a reference measure and not a positive-arity higher-dimensional product.

Let $S$ be the finite normalization, with local DVR centres $S_q$, residue degrees $f_q=[\kappa(q):\kappa(\mathfrak m)]$, and orders $a_q=\operatorname{ord}_q(\mathfrak a)>0$. Every centred semivaluation of a DVR is a positive multiple of its order: write a nonzero element as a power of a uniformizer times a unit, whose value is zero. A support cannot be its maximal ideal, because that would make the boundary ideal infinite. There is no other nonzero prime support in a DVR. Thus G331's normalization presentation identifies the entire downstairs boundary with the finite discrete set
$$v_q=\operatorname{ord}_q/a_q.$$
A regular conductor element has finite value on every branch, so ALL fibres in this curve case are singletons. These are local centres of normalization, not merely minimal components.

Define the reference measure directly from Cartier order on normalized curves:
$$\mu_{\mathfrak a,R}=\sum_q f_q a_q\,\delta_{v_q}.\tag{5}$$
This definition uses actual residue field degrees; there is no generic degree assigned to a vertical component. Every coefficient is positive and finite. The construction is geometric before any ideal-moment comparison.

We prove comparison with an arbitrary actual primary blowup model $Y=\operatorname{Bl}_I R$ and every exceptional REAL Cartier divisor $F$ on it. Since $I S$ is invertible on the semilocal normal curve, the universal property gives a morphism $h:\operatorname{Spec}S\to Y$. It is finite: its graph is closed in $\operatorname{Spec}S\times_R Y$ because $Y$ is separated over $R$, and the projection of this product to $Y$ is finite as a base change of the finite normalization. Its image contains the generic point of every component of $Y$, which is reduced and generically birational on all components by the primary blowup construction in G331. The finite image is closed, hence the map is surjective. It is the normalization of $Y$: locally it is a finite normal birational extension with the same total quotient fields. This special curve argument establishes domination of these actual primary models. It makes no arbitrary higher-dimensional proper-model cofinality assertion.

For an effective integral exceptional Cartier divisor $A$, its independent one-dimensional intersection degree is the proper zero-cycle degree
$$\deg_R[A]=\sum_{y\in\operatorname{Supp}A}\ell_{\mathcal O_{Y,y}}(\mathcal O_{Y,y}/(g_y))\,[\kappa(y):\kappa(\mathfrak m)],$$
where $g_y$ is a regular local equation. The support is a finite subset of the closed fibre: the finite normalization surjects onto it, and its fibre above $\mathfrak m$ is finite. Each relevant local ring is reduced of dimension one, and $A$ cuts a finite-length quotient. Its residue field is finite over the base residue field because it is a closed point of the proper zero-dimensional fibre. This is the usual local Cartier zero-cycle, not a degree defined from valuative moments.

Here is a direct normalization proof of that degree. Put $T=\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ and let $N$ be its finite semilocal normalization. The cokernel $C=N/T$ has finite length, since normalization is generically identical on a reduced curve. Multiplication by the regular element $g=g_y$ in $0\to T\to N\to C\to0$ gives
$$0\to C[g]\to T/gT\to N/gN\to C/gC\to0.$$
For the finite-length module $C$, its multiplication exact sequence gives $\ell(C[g])=\ell(C/gC)$. Therefore $\ell_T(T/gT)=\ell_T(N/gN)$. The DVR factors of $N$ give
$$\ell_T(N/gN)=\sum_{q\mapsto y}[\kappa(q):\kappa(y)]\operatorname{ord}_q(g).$$
Multiplying by $[\kappa(y):\kappa(\mathfrak m)]$ and summing proves
$$\deg_R[A]=\sum_q f_q\operatorname{ord}_q(h^*A).\tag{6}$$
This proof works without normality or Cohen--Macaulay assumptions on $Y$. It uses local actual Cartier equations and the finite normalization, not a replacement by nonnormal Weil coefficients.

Every integral exceptional Cartier $F$ on a primary model can be written as a difference of effective exceptional Cartier divisors by the actual Cartier order-unit assertion of G331; extend (6) by differences and then by finite real linear combinations. Relations cause no ambiguity, since each local order is a homomorphism on actual Cartier divisors. The actual intersection degree of $F$ is therefore
$$\deg_R(F)=\sum_q f_q\operatorname{ord}_q(h^*F).$$
G331's evaluation on the DVR centre is $f_F(v_q)=\operatorname{ord}_q(h^*F)/a_q$, including the negative sign of a negative divisor. Pairing the independently defined (5) gives the exact comparison
$$\int f_F\,d\mu_{\mathfrak a,R}=\deg_R(F).\tag{7}$$
The normalized degree is unchanged by any common primary-model pullback, since its pullback to $S$ is unchanged. Formula (6) also shows that the independent Cartier zero-cycle degree on each such model is that same degree. This proves actual model independence and exact Cartier comparison for every real core presentation and every Cartier test in this curve range.

For a primary ideal $J$, apply one-variable multiplicity additivity (complete Swanson--Huneke 11.2.3--4) to the finite normalization, whose generic rank is one on every reduced component. Equivalently use n4's already proved degree-one formula. The DVR Hilbert function gives $e_{S_q}(JS_q)=\operatorname{ord}_q(J)$, so
$$e_R(J)=\sum_q f_q\operatorname{ord}_q(J)=\int v(J)\,d\mu_{\mathfrak a,R}.$$
Thus (5) agrees with n3's zero-potential moment measure, but its Cartier construction and proof (7) do not rely on assigning moments and then renaming them intersections.

The bounded geometric function class on this finite set is every finite nonpositive branch vector. Indeed each DVR's continuous cone consists of nonpositive constants, obtained from powers of its parameter with real coefficients; the semilocal class is the finite product. The normalization fibres here are singletons, so G331's positivity descent gives all such vectors downstairs. Its actual decreasing completion is every extended nonpositive vector; bounded completed vectors are still finite and hence already continuous. All-zero and mixed-zero profiles are admissible as boundary functions. This says nothing about literal logarithmic radial extensions at a node.

There are no potential variables in (5). Consequently two zero-tuples give the identical measure on every open region of agreement; this is actual open-set locality, albeit a vacuous zero-arity case. Every bounded decreasing-net continuity statement for the zero-tuple is constant equality of measures. It is not advertised as positive-arity Bedford--Taylor locality. Finite continuous tests vary in the usual finite-set norm, so their integrals are continuous as well. Unbounded or bottom potential inputs are not being added: the tuple has zero entries.

For a primary $\mathfrak b$ with $b_q=\operatorname{ord}_q(\mathfrak b)$, the exact change sends $v_q$ to $\operatorname{ord}_q/b_q$ and multiplies its weight by $b_q/a_q$. Hence it is precisely (3), and normalization is (4) with weights $f_q$. On a smooth DVR over its own residue field, $f_q=1$, and (5) has mass $a_q$ at $\operatorname{ord}/a_q$; for the maximal ideal the mass is one. This is the direct dimension-one normalized-local reference convention. For a zero-dimensional reduced local germ, the centred boundary is empty and the only measure is zero, without negative arity.

A concrete residue-degree check prevents replacing $f_q$ by one. Let $k\subset l$ be any finite field extension of degree $d>1$, possibly inseparable, and
$$R=k+t\,l[[t]]\ \subset\ S=l[[t]].$$
Put $A=k[[t]]$. Choosing a $k$-basis $1,\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_d$ of $l$ expresses $R=A\oplus\bigoplus_{i=2}^d tA\alpha_i$, a finite $A$-algebra, so it is Noetherian and excellent. It is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m=tS$ and residue field $k$: a nonzero constant in $k$ gives an inverse still having constant in $k$. Its fraction field is $l((t))$ because $t\alpha/t=\alpha$. Thus $S$ is its finite normalization with GENERIC degree one and RESIDUE degree $d$. The conductor is $tS$: it contains that ideal, and a conductor unit would force $l=k$. For $\mathfrak a=\mathfrak m$, (5) is $d\delta_{\operatorname{ord}_t}$. For $J=t^rS$, $J^N=t^{rN}S$ and a $k$-basis of $R/J^N$ consists of $1$ and all $\alpha_j t^i$, $1\le i<rN$, $1\le j\le d$. Hence
$$\ell_R(R/J^N)=1+d(rN-1),\qquad e_R(J)=dr.$$
This is exactly the moment of (5) and the Cartier divisor degree. A generic-degree-only coefficient would give $r$, which is wrong. The argument does not assume separability.

# n6. Precise degeneracies and a locality diagnostic

Use G331 and n1--n5. These examples distinguish genuine obstructions from missing proofs. They do not assert impossibility of the entire reduced higher-dimensional P12.4 target.

First, nilpotent multiplicity cannot be reconstructed from the reduced boundary and its gauge. Let $R_1=k[[t]]$ and $R_2=k[[t]][\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$, both excellent local rings. The ideal $(t)$ is primary in each, and their reduced gauges and centred semivaluation boundaries are identical: nilpotents have infinite value. Nevertheless
$$\ell_{R_1}(R_1/(t^N))=N,\qquad \ell_{R_2}(R_2/(t^N))=2N.$$
The second quotient has basis $t^i,\epsilon t^i$ for $0\le i<N$, while the first has basis $t^i$. Their Samuel multiplicities are one and two. Thus no assignment depending ONLY on G331's reduced boundary and reduced primary gauge can agree with both unreduced intersection multiplicities. Extra generic-length data are necessary if that different target is requested. Our measure construction deliberately uses $R_{\rm red}$; this is not an obstruction in the explicitly reduced scope.

Second, the degree-$n$ convention has real lower-dimensional degeneracy. Let
$$R=k[[x,y,z]]/(xy,xz)\cong k[[y,z]]\times_k k[[x]],\qquad n=2.$$
It is a reduced excellent complete local ring. The isomorphism sends a series to its restrictions to $x=0$ and $y=z=0$, with equal constant terms; the kernel is $(xy,xz)=(x)\cap(y,z)$. Its normalization is $S=k[[y,z]]\times k[[x]]$, finite because its quotient by $R$ is one copy of $k$. It is normal on both component factors and has the same total quotient fields. Its conductor is the pair of maximal ideals, whose downstairs ideal is $\mathfrak m=(x,y,z)$. Every centred semivaluation has finite conductor value, so the normalized boundary is the disjoint union of the FULL surface boundary and the curve point, with no identified fibres. The pieces are clopen by G331.

Take $\mathfrak a=\mathfrak m$ and $I_N=(y,z,x^N)$. It is proper primary. The rational profile $u_N=-v(I_N)/N$ is constant $-1/N$ on the entire surface piece and $-1$ at the curve point. These profiles converge UNIFORMLY to the finite geometric $C$ function $u$ that is zero on the surface and $-1$ on the curve. This is uniform closure, not an assumed increasing $D$ closure. N4's top-degree normalization formula gives $e_R(I_N,\mathfrak m)=e_{k[[y,z]]}((y,z),(y,z))=1$; the one-dimensional factor has no degree-two coefficient. The last equality follows from the monomial basis count $\ell(k[[y,z]]/(y,z)^t)=t(t+1)/2$. Thus the moment measures of $u_N$ have total mass $1/N$ and their weak limit is the zero measure. By n3, $\nu_{\mathfrak m}(u)=0$ even though $u\ne0$. Formula (4) agrees: the sole top-dimensional input pullback is zero. The lower curve point was retained in the boundary and function class; it was not assigned a vertical generic degree. To seek nonzero curve-local products on that component would require the separate zero-potential arity-one-dimensional convention, not silently adding it to a one-potential dimension-two product.

Third, positivity, multilinearity and bounded continuity do not logically imply actual locality. For a diagnostic independent of any local ring, take the two-point compact discrete space $K=\{x,y\}$, the cone of all nonpositive finite functions, and the positive measure-valued map
$$F(u)=(-u(x)-u(y))\delta_x.$$
It is additive, nonnegative-real homogeneous, uniformly continuous, and continuous for bounded decreasing nets. But $u=(-1,-1)$ and $w=(-1,-2)$ agree on the open set $U=\{x\}$, while $F(u)|_U=2\delta_x$ and $F(w)|_U=3\delta_x$. This is an exact counterexample to the bare implication from those properties to locality. It is NOT claimed to satisfy the primary mixed-multiplicity kernel, to be a geometric singular product, or to disprove locality of n3's measures. It explains why a separate proof, tied to actual local intersections, is still required.

The own program exact_diagnostics.py enumerates only the finite bases and rational gauge arithmetic stated in bounded-evidence-input.json, with no supplied program imported or executed. The observed result was PASS on 48 residue-degree basis cases ($d=2,3$, $r=1,2,3$, $N=1,\ldots,8$), eight nilpotent basis cases ($N=1,\ldots,8$), and 27 two-branch gauge/test combinations, using exact fractions. It checks the residue-degree length slopes, the nilpotent basis counts, and the primary-gauge identity. This is exhaustive on those finite declared arithmetic inputs only. Neither this evidence nor the toy map is a substitute for higher-dimensional Cartier intersection comparison or locality.

# n7. Whole-original decision, unresolved proof coverage, and deliverables

Use qualified G331 and n1--n6. The ENTIRE original P12.4 is NOT solved by this manuscript; candidate=false. This last note makes no complete-solution claim. The positive results and gaps are separated below so that a reviewer can use the partial mathematics without importing a false product theorem.

What is established in the draft proof chain is: an unconditional mixed-multiplicity kernel at every excellent reduced local ring, a unique finite positive moment-measure extension to every real $C$ tuple and every bounded input in the ACTUAL decreasing completion $D$, a weak descending-net theorem whose specified limit belongs to that domain, exact primary-gauge and normalization identities for that construction, and identification with the exact published BFJ operator in its smooth affine CLOSED-germ algebraically closed characteristic-zero range. Every semivaluation support and full conductor fibre is retained. Inputs with zero or mixed-zero coordinates are not excluded; unbounded and bottom inputs are outside this bounded construction. Non-equidimensional rings use the explicitly stated degree-$n$ convention and $n-1$ potential slots.

There is also an actual geometric result for all excellent reduced curves: the zero-potential reference measure (5), independent Cartier degree comparison (6)--(7) on actual primary models for real presentations, model independence, primary-gauge and normalization rules with actual residue-degree weights, and open-set locality and bounded continuity for that zero-arity operator. Dimension zero has the empty-boundary zero measure. N6 supplies a genuine nilpotent-data obstruction and an exact non-equidimensional degeneracy, with their limited conclusions stated.

Two essential higher-dimensional geometric obligations remain unresolved:

1. For every actual negative curve-nef REAL Cartier presentation on an actual primary blowup, prove that the scalar kernel extension is its independent local Cartier intersection, with all nonnormal, non-Cohen--Macaulay, finite-residue-field and non-equidimensional issues handled. In particular, the real $C$ comparison supplied by G331 is a FUNCTION approximation theorem, not an INTERSECTION-continuity theorem. Knowing that section ideals approximate the evaluation uniformly does not prove their multiplicities converge to an independently defined Euler-characteristic intersection. No arbitrary-model cofinality is available. A correct projection and independent-intersection argument on these primary models must be supplied.

2. Prove actual locality on open regions: if each pair $u_i,w_i$ of bounded geometric inputs agrees on an open $U\subset X_{\mathfrak a}$, prove equality of the restrictions of their mixed measures to $U$. Global length polynomials, positivity on tests, uniqueness of moment representation, and weak limits do not establish this. The finite toy diagnostic in n6 shows the general logical implication is false. Even a localized atom formula for core inputs would require a further passage to arbitrary bounded completed inputs; no such passage has been proved here. BFJ Section 4 supplies its exact smooth construction/comparison/continuity, not a singular arbitrary-characteristic locality grant.

Therefore n3's measures are called moment measures, not claimed to be P12.4's actual geometric products. Their algebraic presentation independence must not be relabelled as geometric model-independent intersection theory. The exact full original is left open in dimension at least two. No general obstruction to the reduced target has been proved; missing proof is not impossibility. The nilpotent example obstructs only a boundary-only unreduced multiplicity reconstruction. P12.5 and general P12.6 remain separate.
